title: 🐍 How Did Attackers Hack Microsoft's Own Account? A Stolen Certificate and an AI Tool Behind the Malicious Package!
body: 🐍 How Did Attackers Hack Microsoft's Own Account? A Stolen Certificate and an AI Tool Behind the Malicious Package!

A new investigation revealed how attackers managed to publish two malicious versions of Microsoft's Agent Framework package on the PyPI store on the evening of November 17 — and the answer is more alarming than the package itself: they stole a certificate and private key from the company's internal publishing service.

The service is known as ESRP, the internal system that signs and publishes Microsoft packages. The attackers appear to have seized a client certificate and its private key, then first tried to publish from Amazon servers, but the service's address filters rejected them, before succeeding on a second attempt from an address owned by Microsoft itself. It is still unknown how the certificate was stolen in the first place.

As for the tool used, it calls itself Kern — an open-source framework for AI penetration testing. The attackers prepared the package in a temporary folder and sent a connectivity test signal before publishing; they even tried the theft software on their own machines first, and that test captured the settings of an open-source coding assistant running a model from the GLM family.

Analysis by JFrog revealed that the malicious package was not built in Microsoft's pipelines at all: it was repackaged locally just nine minutes before upload, on a machine with a UTC+8 timezone — East Asia time. The second version, 1.26.2, was cleverer: it restored the original clean file to its place and moved the malicious payload to a new file, so a file comparison would not detect it.

Despite the package's size — downloaded about 190,000 times a month — the actual damage appears limited: the data-exfiltration channel was a free service accepting only 100 requests, and it captured 50 requests — 4 from the attackers' own machines and 29 from test and scanning environments — leaving 17 requests representing just three successful thefts of victims' data. The Chainguard service also stopped the first version just 48 seconds after it was published.

Simply put: the attack was not just a tainted package, but the theft of the official publishing keys themselves, carried out by an AI tool — and it nearly succeeded, had the free exfiltration channel not filled up quickly.
Are public store checks enough to protect developers, or has trust in official packages themselves come to need rethinking?
